question: Why are you exploring new opportunities?
answer: I left KKday in August 2026. The Shanghai office cut many jobs, and I was one of them. So I'm using this time to choose carefully. I'm looking for three things. First, AI on mobile is the core product, not a side feature. Second, I own the Android experience from start to finish. Third, a small team where I work closely with backend and AI engineers. At KKday, I worked on both sides of an AI feature. How the planner built an answer, and how a traveler actually used it. I want more of that, on Android. ActAI fits all three.

question: Why do you want to join ActAI specifically?
answer: There are three reasons. First, ActAI's product and my own product share a similar direction. In May, I started designing an AI agent in my spare time. It's called Cabinet. For example, I plan a three-day trip. I need to check my calendar, the weather, and my budget. Checking them one by one is slow. And I can easily miss something. Cabinet thinks of all this for me. Then it gives me a good plan. ActAI builds proactive AI products for everyone. People don't need to write complex prompts. The first product starts with communication. It puts an agent at the center. The goal is to make coordination between people easier. Here is my understanding. Friends agree on a Friday meeting in a chat. Then the agent sets it up for them. So I have real interest in this direction. I also have real experience. Second, ActAI needs someone to make AI fast and stable on Android. That's my strength. I have ten years of experience, mostly on Android. At KKday, I cut the first-screen loading time on Android. It went from three seconds to under one second. I also showed AI results step by step. Users didn't have to wait. At Ping An Haoxue, I improved a classroom app on cheap Android tablets. It ran smoothly, even on low-end devices. Third, I want to join a startup like ActAI. In a startup, nobody writes every detail for you. You need to bring structure, make decisions, and move fast. I like this way of working. I can help shape the product. And I own the results. I've done this before. At Kezhi, the product was brand new. I reported to the CTO. I was the only Android engineer. I built the base of the Android app from zero. Our team built the first version in four weeks. So I want to build a great product with ActAI. I want people to trust it and use it every day.

question: Why did you leave your last three companies?
answer: Just to be precise, two of them were layoffs, and one was my own decision. At KKday, the business line was shrinking. Most of the people they kept had been there longer than me. I'd joined about a year and a half earlier. My performance was in the top 30% of the Tour team, so I don't think it was about my work. Debon was similar. The business had struggled for two years, and our Android team went from three people to one. They kept the longest-serving engineer. Before I left, my work had shipped and I handed everything over cleanly. Kezhi was different. After the team was disbanded, there was no real product work left, and the company's future was unclear. Many people left, and I decided to leave too.

question: What people or working styles do you dislike working with, especially in your most recent role?
answer: I don't like it when people change something others depend on, and don't tell them. Once, we were building a booking page. The backend changed how stock status was returned, but didn't tell the Android side. So some packages that were in stock couldn't be selected. I compared the real response with what we had agreed, and found the change. Then I worked with the backend engineer on the fix. We retested every package that was affected. After that, we agreed on one rule. For any shared API change, explain what changed first, and send sample data. That way, the app side can check the impact. Later, when they changed these APIs, they sent sample data first. So we found what both sides needed to change before testing together. I understand things get missed under deadlines. When I do backend work, I remind myself of this too. When your change affects others, telling them early is a habit I value.

question: What kind of manager do you work best with?
answer: I work best with a manager who sets a clear goal and then trusts me on the details. At Kezhi I reported to the CTO, and he told me what the first version had to do. He didn't tell me how to build it. I set up the Android base myself, and our team shipped the first version in four weeks. I also like a manager who gives direct feedback. My KKday lead once told me to keep the scope of my changes under control. It was fair, and I changed how I plan releases after that. What's hard for me is a manager who changes priorities but doesn't say what matters most. I'd rather ask early: what must work first? Then I can move my time there and tell the team what changed.

question: What are your strengths and weaknesses?
answer: My main strength is following a problem across the app and the backend. At KKday, sometimes the AI reply didn't fit what the app could show. I could fix both the reply format and the fallback. My weak spot is model training. I'm better at putting AI into products. I can own the app side and the test cases. For model quality, I'd work with the ML engineer.

question: What do you understand about the product we're building, and what would you still need to learn?
answer: I understand ActAI as a voice and text communication app with an agent at the center. People shouldn't need to write long prompts. They say what they want, and the assistant helps get it done. For example, friends agree on a Friday meeting in a chat, and the agent sets it up for them. The goal is to make coordination between people easier. I also know the team is small and based in Beijing, and I'd work closely with the founder and CTO. What I'd still need to learn is the product details. I don't know yet which tasks you want to handle first, or how you decide when the assistant should act alone and when it should ask the user first. I'd also need to learn your backend and AI setup, and how the Android app talks to it. And I'd need to learn how you measure success, like time saved or how often people correct the assistant.

question: How do you feel about work-life balance? What if priorities change halfway through a sprint?
answer: I care about balance, but I don't treat it as a reason to slow down. I plan my week around the moments when other people need me. If priorities change halfway through a sprint, I ask what must work for users on launch day. Then I move my time there and tell the team what changed and when they can test it. A short push is fine. But if every week feels like launch week, I'd raise it and we'd fix the plan together.

question: We look for 7H: head, hands, hustle, humility, heart, hunger and habits. Which one describes you best? Give an example.
answer: Hustle describes me best. At Kezhi, I was the only Android engineer, and the product was brand new. I built the base of the app from zero, and our team shipped the first version in four weeks. I also handled testing and releases myself. When something was unclear, I didn't wait for a full plan. I made a call, shipped it, and fixed it fast. That's how I like to work in a startup.

question: If you work remotely, how do you keep yourself accountable daily and weekly? What is on your personal scoreboard?
answer: At KKday, I worked remotely some of the time. I plan each week around handoff points. For a booking page, I first agree when we test with the backend, and when QA gets it. Then I plan my own coding time around that. Each day follows those points. If we test with the backend in the afternoon, I get the flow working in the morning and list the API issues. So we can fix them together right away. My updates are specific. For example: "The page is done. The main flow works. Empty stock is left. I'll check it with the backend tomorrow." That way, QA knows what they can test first. Across time zones, I'd write the questions, sample data, and what needs confirming clearly in advance. Then we'd use the overlap hours to discuss them together. When something urgent comes in, I explain the trade-off. For example: "Today I'll fix the checkout bug. The page redesign moves one day. I'll send the new QA date." Then I confirm it with my lead. Each week, I check three things. Did I deliver what I promised? How much was missed or redone? Did anyone wait on me?

question: Would you deliver bad news to your team early or later?
answer: Early. The sooner the team knows, the more time they have to adjust. But I bring the problem and a suggestion together. At Debon Securities, I was rebuilding part of our trading app. It was planned to ship with that week's release. During testing, I found some old pages had a broken back button with the new navigation. I hadn't checked every page yet. But it could already affect the release. So I told the project manager that same day. I said: "Some pages are confirmed broken. I'm still checking the rest. If this ships this week, we may not have time to test it fully. I suggest we keep the old pages, and move this change to the next release. Everything else can ship as planned. I'll update you tomorrow afternoon on the impact and the fix." We changed the release scope. Everything else shipped on time. My change shipped later, after it was fixed and tested. To me, telling early gives the team time to choose. And I don't just report the problem. I keep pushing the fix, and keep everyone updated.

question: What are your salary expectations?

question: What is your current or previous compensation?
answer: At KKday, I earned RMB 26,000 a month, for 13 months. I also got a yearly bonus of about RMB 50,000. So my fixed pay was RMB 338,000 a year. With the bonus, it was about RMB 388,000. At Kezhi, I earned RMB 31,000 a month, for 12 months. That's RMB 372,000 a year.

question: What's your minimum?
answer: I'd rather not give a single number first. Could you share the base range for this role, plus the bonus and equity structure? Then I can tell you clearly whether it works for me.

question: When can you start?
answer: I can start quite soon. I left KKday in August, so I have no notice period to serve. I'd just need a few days to sort things out, and I can confirm the exact date against your target start date.

question: Can you work with an international team in English?
answer: Yes, I can. I worked in an international team at KKday, and I can explain my work clearly in English. I'm comfortable in meetings and in writing. If the team speaks fast, I may ask someone to repeat a point, but I won't miss the meaning.

question: How would you explain the idea of 'Cursor for everyone' in practical user terms?

question: What would you want to learn about our product before deciding to join?

question: Is there anything in your timeline or references that you'd like to clarify?

question: How has your agent or RAG work changed the way you build mobile experiences?
answer: My agent and RAG work changed three things in how I build mobile experiences. First, I design for partial answers. At KKday, the AI trip planner streams the plan day by day. The first day's card shows up while the rest is still being made. So the user never stares at a blank screen. On Android, I show what's ready and keep a clear loading state for the rest. Second, I design for things going wrong. AI replies can be incomplete or badly shaped. So the app checks the response, and when it fails, it shows a safe fallback and lets the user retry or edit. At KKday, the backend checked the structure and product IDs, and retried with the specific error. Third, I design for user control. In Cabinet, the assistant only proposes changes to the calendar or reminders. Nothing happens until the user taps to apply it. That habit comes straight from RAG: when the material isn't enough, say so instead of guessing. So the biggest change is this. I stopped treating AI as a text box. I treat it as a slow, sometimes wrong partner, and the app has to keep the user in control the whole time.

question: What would you need to learn to become effective in this role?
answer: Two things. First, I'd get real hands-on with on-device ML, like TensorFlow Lite and ML Kit. I know the app side well, but I haven't shipped a model on the phone myself. Second, I'd learn your codebase and your AI APIs fast, so I can own a feature end to end in the first few weeks. My strength is putting AI into a product people use.

question: Tell me about a project you owned from an unclear problem through delivery.
answer: At KKday, I owned the AI trip planner from an unclear problem through delivery. The problem was vague: planning a trip takes too long. Users had to check budgets, search products and build the plan by hand. I was the technical lead of a five-person team. I designed the agent and built the core backend. We let users type something like "Tokyo, three days, 5,000 yuan" and get a plan they could book. The first day's card shows up while the rest is still being made. The system now handles about 300,000 planning tasks a day.

question: Which achievement are you most proud of, and how did you measure its impact?
answer: The one I'm most proud of is the product page at KKday. When a traveller tapped a tour, it took about a second before the options and prices appeared. That's long enough to feel slow. I looked into it and found the app was reading the same data again and again. It also did heavy calculations at the moment the page opened. So I simplified the data and prepared the price and stock lookups in advance. I moved the heavy work into the background and cached the results. It went from about one second to about 300 milliseconds. I measured it in two ways. Offline, I marked when the screen finished drawing, using FrameMetrics and JankStats, and checked it with Perfetto. Online, I used event tracking and looked at the percentiles. I don't have conversion numbers for it. The impact I can point to is the waiting time users feel.

question: Tell me about a time you solved a problem outside your formal responsibilities.
answer: At Kezhi, I was the only Android engineer, so testing and releases weren't anyone else's job. I took them on myself. I set up the build and release steps, tested each feature before it went out, and handled the store releases. The team shipped the first version in four weeks. Nobody asked me to own that. I just saw it needed doing, and I did it.

question: Tell me about a project that did not achieve the result you expected.
answer: The project that didn't land as I hoped was the RAG question-answering system at Kezhi. We built it for many school subjects, and the first version looked fine in demos. But when we tested it with real student questions, some answers were correct in content but pulled from the wrong grade or chapter. So the answer didn't match what the student was actually learning. I dug into the search step. The problem was that we searched too widely. So I changed it to narrow down by subject, grade and chapter first, then look for the answer. I retested the questions that had failed, and some found the right chapter. I also checked that other questions didn't get worse. What I took from it is that a good demo doesn't mean it works. I should test with real questions much earlier, and check the source of the answer, not just whether it sounds right.

question: Tell me about a time you had to move fast.
answer: At Kezhi, our team built the first features of an exam app in four weeks. I owned the base of the Android app. I also helped put features together. Some screens were in the app, and some were web pages. So I set up routing between modules. I also made a way to show web pages inside the app. That way, both kinds of features made the first version.

question: What would you do if you couldn't stop feature work to fix reliability?
answer: I'd protect the release first, then fix reliability in small pieces. I'd agree with my lead on what must be stable for users, like sending a message. Then I'd cut or delay one lower-value feature to make room. I'd also fix the worst reliability issue in small steps alongside feature work, not as a big separate project. If the problem keeps growing, I'd show the data, like crash or failure rates, and ask the team to choose the trade-off openly.

question: How do you handle a short period of intense work before a critical launch?
answer: I'm fine with a short intense push before a launch. I'd agree with my lead on what must work on day one, and what can wait. Then I'd focus on that, and tell the team what changed and when they can test it. I'd also keep an eye on how many days it lasts. A few hard weeks are fine, but if every week feels like launch week, I'd raise it and we'd fix the plan together.

question: How would you respond if a founder changed direction after two weeks of your work?
answer: I'd ask what changed and why, before I touch any code. Then I'd check what still works and what we can keep. At Kezhi, the product was new and priorities moved fast, so I learned to keep the base of the app flexible. I'd tell the team what we keep and what we drop, and give a new date. If the change is big, I'd say so honestly. I'd rather lose two weeks than build the wrong thing for two months.

question: Tell me about a time you chose a simpler solution to ship sooner.
answer: At KKday, our AI trip planner had to show a plan while it was still being generated. The full design was complex. So I chose a simpler first version. I sent the plan day by day, so the first day's cards appeared right away. Users didn't wait for the whole plan. That shipped sooner, and we could improve it later with real feedback.

question: Tell me about a mistake you made that affected other people.
answer: At KKday, I made a mistake that slowed down QA. I finished a booking page on time. But I only planned when the code would be done. I left all the API checks to the last day. When we tested with the backend, empty stock didn't match what the app expected. Both sides had to change and retest, so QA got it late. In my weekly review, I saw the cause. Before coding, I now ask the backend for sample data: normal cases, in stock, and out of stock. I list problems early, and I plan separate time for testing and fixes. After that, we found most data issues before joint testing. There was less last-minute rework, and QA dates were easier to predict.

question: What would you do if a stakeholder asked you to present an uncertain result as a confirmed improvement?
answer: I'd say no, I can't present it as confirmed. I'd show what we actually measured and how sure we are. Then I'd say what we still need to check before we call it an improvement. If they still want a strong claim, I'd ask them to label it as early data, not a result.

question: Tell me about a time you changed your mind after receiving new evidence.
answer: At Kezhi, I changed how I built the RAG search after real test questions showed a problem. At first, the AI answered from memory. Some answers looked fine, but they used content from the wrong grade. So I changed the search. First I narrowed it down by subject, grade and chapter. Then I looked for the answer. I retested the questions that had failed, and some now found the right chapter. I also checked that other questions didn't get worse. That evidence changed my mind, so I kept the new way.

question: Tell me about a disagreement with a manager, product partner or engineer.
answer: At Debon Securities, I disagreed with our project manager about a release. I was rebuilding part of the trading app, and testing showed the back button broke on some old pages. I wanted to delay that change. He wanted to ship it with the week's release. I showed him what was confirmed broken and what I was still checking. I said we could keep the old pages and move my change to the next release. Everything else would ship on time. He agreed. My change shipped later, after it was fixed and tested.

question: How did you handle coordination between the backend and the app at KKday?
answer: At KKday, we agreed on the API format before coding. I asked the backend for sample data first: normal cases, in stock, and out of stock. Then I checked the real responses against what we agreed. When the AI trip planner needed a new field, we defined the response format together. I also set one rule. For any shared API change, explain what changed first, and send sample data. That way, the app side can check the impact before testing. If something still broke, I compared the real response with the agreed format, found the change, and fixed it with the backend engineer.

question: Tell me about a time you helped a teammate who was struggling.
answer: At Ping An Haoxue, one of our Android engineers was behind on the classroom SDK work. He was quiet about it, and I only found out when his part was late. So I sat with him and asked what was blocking him. The audio and video parts were new to him, and he was afraid to ask. I broke his task into smaller pieces and paired with him on the first one. I also asked him to send me a short update every day. After that he finished his part, and the two apps shared the same classroom code.

question: What kind of environment would make it hard for you to perform?
answer: I'm fine with fast changes and a process that's still being built. What makes it hard is when poor communication keeps causing rework, and nothing changes. For example, developers and QA work from different versions of the same feature. They only find out near the end. That happens sometimes, and it's normal. When it does, I put the latest decisions and changes in one shared place. I ask the people involved to confirm it. A simple fix first. I don't expect a team where everything is already set up. I'm happy to help build how we work. What matters to me is that when we find a problem, we adjust together, so it happens less next time.

question: Tell me about a time asynchronous communication prevented or caused a problem.
answer: At KKday, async communication caused a problem for me. The backend changed how stock status was returned, but didn't tell the Android side. So some packages that were in stock couldn't be selected. I compared the real response with what we had agreed, and found the change. Then I worked with the backend engineer on the fix. After that, we agreed on one rule. For any shared API change, explain what changed first, and send sample data. Later, when they changed these APIs, they sent sample data first. So we found what both sides needed to change before testing together.

question: How would you work with a team spread across several time zones?
answer: I'd plan my week around the overlap hours. I'd write questions, sample data and what needs confirming clearly in advance, so people can read them when they start. Then we'd use the shared hours to decide together. Each day I'd send a short, specific update, like what's done and what's blocked. If something urgent comes in, I'd explain the trade-off and give a new date. I haven't worked across many time zones before, but at KKday I worked remotely some of the time, and these habits are the same.

question: How do you handle a discussion in English when you don't fully understand a requirement or you disagree with it?
answer: I'd say it plainly. I'd say I didn't fully understand, and ask them to explain that part again. Then I'd repeat it back in my own words, so we both know I got it right. If I disagree, I'd say what I see and why, and give a concrete example. I'd keep it about the work, not the person. At KKday, I worked with people in other countries, and English was our shared language. Asking early is much better than guessing and building the wrong thing.

question: Do you do a weekly review? Give me an example of how it changed your approach.
answer: Yes, I do a weekly review. Each week, I look at what didn't go as planned, and what I should change. Once, I finished a booking page on time. But on the day we tested with the backend, we found a problem. When stock was empty, the API data didn't match what the app expected. Both sides had to change and retest. So QA got it late. In the review, I saw my mistake. I only planned when the code would be done. I left all the API issues to the last day. So I changed how I work. Before coding, I ask the backend for sample data. Normal cases, in stock, and out of stock. I list problems early. And I plan separate time for testing and fixes. After that, we found most data issues before testing together. There was less last-minute rework, and QA dates were easier to predict. What changed was how I judge progress. A finished page is just one step. It's done when it works with the backend and QA can test it.

question: What is the most useful critical feedback you have received?
answer: The most useful critical feedback I got was from my manager at KKday. He told me to keep the scope of my changes under control. There was a feature I could have built on the existing architecture. It needed quite a lot of code, so I wanted to improve that part of the architecture at the same time. But that made the release take longer. That taught me that even a good long-term improvement needs the right timing. Now I describe the feature and the architecture work separately. Then the team and I agree whether it's worth doing both in this release.

question: Tell me about something difficult you learned recently and applied in practice.
answer: The most useful thing I learned recently was how to make an AI answer look up real material before it replies. At Kezhi, we built a Q&A tool for many school subjects. I started with a few textbooks and got the basic flow working. Then I tested it with real questions. Some answers looked fine, but they used content from the wrong grade. So I changed how it searched. First I narrow down by subject, grade and chapter. Then I look for the answer. I retested the questions that had failed, and some now found the right chapter. I also checked that other questions didn't get worse. I used the same idea later at KKday, when I built the RAG system there.

question: Tell me about a time user feedback changed your engineering priorities.
answer: Honestly, I didn't have formal user feedback data on my recent work. On the KKday product page, I checked the experience myself by going through the booking flow. Here, I'd watch where users drop off and where they correct the assistant, and fix the step that causes the most corrections first.

question: How do you decide when AI is useful and when a simpler approach is better?
answer: I use a simple test. AI is worth it when the input is open and messy, like a free sentence about a trip. A simple approach is better when the rules are clear and the answer must be exact. At KKday, the AI trip planner was a good fit. A traveler typed "Tokyo, three days, 5,000 yuan." The AI pulled out the destination, budget and days, then built a plan. A fixed form couldn't do that well. But price and stock were not AI work. I calculated those with plain code, in advance. The AI should never guess a price. So I keep AI for understanding and planning, and normal code for numbers and rules.

question: How do you use AI coding tools while staying accountable for what you ship?
answer: I write the core architecture myself, and I review and test everything the tools generate before it goes in. For example, in CabinetAI I built the base framework by hand and used AI tools only for the simpler screens. I read every change, run it, and check the edge cases myself. The tool saves typing time, but I stay responsible for what ships.

question: Imagine an AI communication feature gives a misleading answer or captures audio unexpectedly. What would you do?
answer: I'd treat those as two different problems. A misleading answer is a product and trust problem. Unexpected audio capture is a privacy and permission problem, and that one is more serious. For a misleading answer, I'd first make the app show where the answer came from. In CabinetAI, RAG answers cite the original text, and when the material is thin, the assistant says so instead of guessing. I'd also let the user correct it in one tap, and keep that correction. Then I'd add the bad case to a test set, so we catch it next time. At KKday, I built a review pipeline with prompt versions and regression tests, so we could replay old cases and see if a fix broke something else. For unexpected audio capture, I'd stop and check it straight away. The app should only record after a clear action from the user, and show that it's recording. The microphone permission should be asked at the moment it's needed, not at sign-up. Audio should not be kept longer than needed, and the user should be able to see and delete what was kept. If we found a real bug, I'd turn the feature off with a remote switch, tell the team and the users honestly, and fix the cause before turning it back on. So my rule is simple. The assistant can be wrong, but it must never hide that it's unsure, and it must never listen without the user knowing.

question: How would you evaluate a counteroffer?

I'd also like to know how Android, backend and ML share ownership when a feature fails. That's it, really. The product direction is the reason I'm here.

question: What would you want us to remember about you after this conversation?

question: Is there anything we haven't covered that would help us evaluate your fit fairly?

question: Which AI products do you use every day, and what frustrates you about them?

question: What do you think of Meta AI in WhatsApp or Gemini in Messages? Why would people switch to ActAI?
answer: Their biggest advantage is that people don't have to switch apps. So for ActAI to win, it has to fix a problem people hit again and again, and the benefit has to be big enough to be worth installing another app. From what I've seen, those assistants mostly wait for you to ask. ActAI's idea is to help before you have to ask. In CabinetAI, I've been working on the same question: once someone says what they want, can we cut out the copying and manual steps? For example, if a voice message mentions a meeting time, some materials to prepare and a deadline, the assistant should turn that into a short list for me to confirm, and then carry on. I shouldn't have to listen again and type it all in. I don't expect people to leave WhatsApp on day one. More likely, they start using ActAI for one task, find it saves them steps every day, and gradually move more conversations over. So what matters to me isn't how many AI features there are. It's whether getting from saying it to getting it done feels natural, fast and reliable. That's where I want to bring my Android and AI experience together.

question: How would you know if that kind of assistant is actually working?
answer: I'd look at three things: how much time it saves before something is agreed, how often people have to correct it, and whether they come back the next week. If people keep correcting it, the extra steps might cost more time than it saves.

question: An assistant that reads people's chats. How do you think about privacy and trust?
answer: I think what people fear most is something they said privately showing up somewhere they didn't expect. Say I talk to a friend about changing jobs, and later the AI mentions it in a message it drafts to my colleague. Nothing leaked, but I'd stop trusting it. So consent can't be a single checkbox at sign-up. People should see which chats the AI can read and what it keeps, and be able to take that back at any time. A deleted memory should never come back. And anything that affects other people, like sending a message or sharing something, should show me the content and the recipient first. To me, a trustworthy assistant makes its limits clear and leaves the user in control.

question: Can you explain something technical you built, in simple English?
answer: At Kezhi, I worked on an AI tool that answers students' questions using their learning materials. Instead of asking the AI to answer from memory, we first find the right content in the textbooks. We narrow the search by subject, grade and chapter, so we don't mix up different courses. Then we give that content to the AI to help it answer. It's like an open-book exam: find the right material first, then explain the answer. That way, the answers stay accurate and match what the students are actually learning.

question: How do you keep an app stable in production? Have you worked on crashes?
answer: Yes, I've worked on crashes a lot. At Debon Securities, I tracked and fixed crashes in production. Our team cut the crash rate from about 1% to about 0.1%. We tracked it in Bugly, as crashes per app launch. Most crashes were null pointers, out-of-memory errors, WebView crashes, and problems on certain phone models. We fixed them group by group, starting with the most common. For stability in general, I do three things. First, I catch errors early and report them with enough detail to find the cause. Second, I fix the most common crashes first, because they affect the most users. Third, I test on low-end phones, not just my own device. At KKday, I also made the app feel stable when the AI was still working. The first card showed up early, and the rest came in after. If a reply failed the checks, we retried with the exact error, and had a fallback after that. So users never saw a broken screen.
